\chapter{Months}
\label{ch:hi-months}
\hlchaptermodality{16}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the twelve months in Hindi and explain why the festivals move against the Gregorian calendar.}

Say \hi{जनवरी} through \hi{दिसंबर}, then name Chaitra and Vaiśākh and explain that the festivals are dated by Vikram Samvat instead.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[janvarī farvarī mārc aprail maī jūn …]{\hi{जनवरी} to \hi{दिसंबर} — borrowed names, and a second calendar underneath}

\label{lesson:HI-C16-mahine}



\begin{quote}
Like Arabic, Hindi doesn't have just \textbf{one} set of months — everyday civil life and traditional/religious life run on \textbf{two different calendars}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — The Gregorian months — recent, borrowed}
For dates, school, business, and government, Hindi uses month names borrowed straightforwardly from \textbf{English}:

\textbf{\hi{जनवरी}, \hi{फ़रवरी}, \hi{मार्च}, \hi{अप्रैल}, \hi{मई}, \hi{जून}, \hi{जुलाई}, \hi{अगस्त}, \hi{सितंबर}, \hi{अक्टूबर}, \hi{नवंबर}, \hi{दिसंबर}} (\emph{janvarī, farvarī, mārc, aprail, maī, jūn, julāī, agast, sitambar, aktūbar, navambar, disambar}) — you can hear \textquotedblleft{}January,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}March,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}August\textquotedblright{} right through the Hindi pronunciation. This is a modern civil borrowing, not an ancient Sanskrit system.

\subsection*{You'll want to know — Be honest: the traditional calendar is a genuinely different structure}
Hindu tradition keeps its \textbf{own}, much older lunisolar calendar — \textbf{\hi{विक्रम} \hi{संवत्}} (\emph{Vikram Samvat}) — with twelve \textbf{different} month names: \textbf{\hi{चैत्र}, \hi{वैशाख}, \hi{ज्येष्ठ}, \hi{आषाढ़}, \hi{श्रावण}, \hi{भाद्रपद}, \hi{आश्विन}, \hi{कार्तिक}, \hi{मार्गशीर्ष}, \hi{पौष}, \hi{माघ}, \hi{फाल्गुन}} (\emph{Chaitra, Vaiśākh, Jyeṣṭha, Āṣāḍh, Śrāvaṇ, Bhādrapad, Āśvin, Kārtik, Mārgaśīrṣ, Pauṣ, Māgh, Phālgun}).

This isn't just a second set of labels for the same twelve solar months — these months are tied to the \textbf{six-ṛtu} seasonal calendar from the seasons lesson (in the traditional/classical scheme, each pair of Vikram Samvat months corresponds to one of the six \emph{ṛtu}), and major festivals (Holi, Diwali, and many others) are dated by \textbf{this} calendar, not the Gregorian one — which is why their Gregorian-calendar date shifts from year to year.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}janvarī, mārc, agast\textquotedblright{} — hear the borrowed English names
  \item the traditional calendar — \textquotedblleft{}Chaitra, Vaiśākh, Jyeṣṭha\textquotedblright{}
  \item the honest point — festivals shift on the Gregorian calendar because they're dated by Vikram Samvat instead
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where do Hindi's everyday civil month names come from? (\textbf{Borrowed from English} — \emph{janvarī, mārc, agast}...) What traditional calendar runs alongside it, and what is it tied to? (\textbf{Vikram Samvat} — tied to the \textbf{six ṛtu} seasons, not the four-season Western frame.) Why do festivals like Holi and Diwali fall on different Gregorian dates each year? (\textbf{They're dated by Vikram Samvat}, a different calendar system entirely.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[u]{\hi{◌ु} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:HI-S120-vowel-sign-u}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \hi{ष} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \hi{◌ु}}
\textbf{\hi{◌ु}} — \emph{u}.

It is a \textbf{vowel sign}. It is not a letter and never stands alone: it attaches to a consonant and \textbf{replaces} the \emph{a} built into it with \emph{u}. Replaces, not adds — the \emph{a} is gone.

Where it sits: a small hook below the consonant.

Worked through: \textbf{\hi{त}} + \textbf{\hi{◌ु}} = \textbf{\hi{तु}} — \emph{tu}.

You already say these, and every one of them has \hi{◌ु} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\hi{शुक्रिया}} — thanks (shukriyā — everyday, Persian/Arabic-derived)
  \item \textbf{\hi{आप} / \hi{तुम}} — you (respectful / familiar)
  \item \textbf{\hi{ख़ुशी}} — happiness / pleased to meet you
  \item \textbf{\hi{सोमवार} \hi{मंगलवार} \hi{बुधवार} \hi{गुरुवार} \hi{शुक्रवार}} — Monday–Friday
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \hi{◌ु} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \hi{◌ु} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \hi{◌ु} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\hi{शुक्रिया}  ·  \hi{नमस्ते}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \hi{◌ु} three times, saying \emph{u} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page and find \hi{◌ु} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \hi{◌ु}? What vowel does it put on the consonant it attaches to — and what does it take off? (\textbf{Puts \emph{u} on; takes the built-in \emph{a} off.}) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ṃ]{\hi{◌ं} — the dot above the line}

\label{lesson:HI-S148-sign-anusvara}



\begin{quote}
The hook from before sat \textbf{below} the consonant. Say what it did.

Today's mark sits \textbf{above the head-line}, and you have been reading it since your first week.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \hi{◌ं}}
\textbf{\hi{◌ं}} — the \textbf{anusvāra}. A single dot, sitting on top of the shirorekhā.

It sends the syllable \textbf{through the nose}. It is not a vowel and it does not replace one: the vowel stays exactly as it was, and the air changes route.

Worked through: \textbf{\hi{स}} + \textbf{\hi{◌ं}} = \textbf{\hi{सं}}.

\subsection*{Script: you have been saying it all along}
Look at the dot above the line in each of these:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\hi{मैं}} — I
  \item \textbf{\hi{हैं}} — are
  \item \textbf{\hi{मिलेंगे}} — we will meet
  \item \textbf{\hi{में}} — in
  \item \textbf{\hi{हिंदी}} — Hindi
\end{itemize}

These are not decorative words. \textbf{\hi{मैं}} and \textbf{\hi{हैं}} are how you say who you are and how things stand, and you have been reading that dot in them without a lesson ever naming it.

There is a second nasal mark, a crescent with a dot inside it, and which of the two a word takes depends on what else is sitting above the letter.

\subsection*{Writing: \hi{◌ं} — copy what you see}
Draw the letter and its head-line as you already do. Then put one dot \textbf{above the line}, over the middle of the letter.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these two words and find the dot above the line
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\hi{मैं}  ·  \hi{हैं}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \hi{मैं} three times, saying \emph{maĩ} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Say it:} whether this mark changes the vowel or the air
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does \textbf{\hi{◌ं}} sit? (Above the head-line.) What does it change? (The route of the air, not the vowel.) Name the word for \emph{I} that carries it.
\end{tcolorbox}
